title: Contractualism: What We Owe to Each Other
subtitle: Morality as the principles no one could reasonably reject
objectives: By the end you will be able to distinguish contractarianism (Hobbes, Gauthier) from contractualism (Scanlon) and explain why the difference matters.
By the end you will be able to state Scanlon's reasonable rejection test and apply it to a worked example.
By the end you will be able to explain the individualist restriction and the Transmitter Room case, and how contractualism handles aggregation.
By the end you will be able to compare contractualism with utilitarianism and Kantian ethics and assess its main objections.
hook:
Imagine you are about to do something that will affect other people: cancel a promise, take the last seat on a lifeboat, adopt a policy that helps most residents of a town but harms a few. Picture each affected person standing in front of you and asking, "Why should I accept this?" Could you give each of them an answer they could not reasonably refuse?

That imagined conversation is the heart of **contractualism**, a moral theory developed by the Harvard philosopher T. M. Scanlon in an essay of 1982 and his book *What We Owe to Each Other* (1998). It belongs to a family of theories you met on Day 42 with Hobbes, on Day 53 with Rousseau and on Day 82 with Rawls: theories that ground principles in some kind of agreement. But Scanlon's version turns the social contract from a theory of the state into a theory of right and wrong itself. Its guiding idea is that morality is, at bottom, a matter of being able to justify ourselves to one another.

sections.heading: Two Kinds of Contract
sections.body:
Agreement-based moral theories come in two very different families, and the names are confusingly similar.

**Contractarianism** descends from Hobbes (Day 42). Morality is a set of rules that self-interested people would agree to for **mutual advantage**. In the state of nature, everyone is worse off; by agreeing to restrain ourselves, each of us gains. The most rigorous modern version is David Gauthier's *Morals by Agreement* (1986), which used game theory to argue that rational maximizers would choose to become **constrained maximizers**: people disposed to cooperate with other cooperators even when cheating would pay in a particular case, because such people are trusted and get the benefits of cooperation. On this view, morality is rational self-interest wisely understood.

Contractarianism has a striking advantage: it explains why anyone should be moral using only something nobody doubts they care about, their own interests. It needs no queer moral facts (ethics-1). But it has a notorious problem. Agreements for mutual advantage include only those with something to offer or something to threaten. Infants, many animals, future generations, and people with severe disabilities have little bargaining power. A pure mutual-advantage contract seems to give them no moral standing in their own right, which strikes most people as a disqualifying result.

**Contractualism**, Scanlon's view, descends instead from Kant (Day 56) and Rousseau (Day 53). The parties are not bargaining for advantage. They are motivated by a desire to find principles that others, similarly motivated, could not reasonably reject. The contract is not a deal but an ideal of **mutual justifiability**. Scanlon calls this ideal a relationship of **mutual recognition**: standing in a relation with others in which each can justify their actions to the rest. Because the test is what each person could reasonably reject, not what each person could extract by bargaining, the weak count as much as the strong.

Rawls's original position (Day 82) is a cousin of both. His parties are self-interested but placed behind a **veil of ignorance**, so that impartiality is built into the setup. Scanlon's method differs: he does not hide information from the parties, but asks directly what principles fully informed people could reasonably reject.

sections.heading: The Reasonable Rejection Test
sections.body:
Scanlon's formula is precise and worth quoting in full:

> An act is wrong if its performance under the circumstances would be disallowed by any set of principles for the general regulation of behaviour that no one could reasonably reject as a basis for informed, unforced general agreement.

Let us take this apart.
- **Principles for the general regulation of behaviour.** We evaluate not single acts but the principles that would permit them. Like Kant's universalizability test, this forces us to consider what would happen if everyone in a similar situation acted the same way.
- **Reasonably reject.** The test is not whether anyone *would* reject a principle (some people reject everything), but whether they could do so *reasonably*: with good reasons that others motivated by the same ideal would have to acknowledge.
- **Informed, unforced.** Agreement achieved by deception or coercion does not count.

The method is **comparative**. To decide whether a principle can be reasonably rejected, compare the burdens it would impose on the person most affected with the burdens that alternative principles would impose on others. A principle is rejectable if someone has a stronger objection to it than anyone has to the alternatives.

A worked example: **promising**. Suppose you promise to help your friend move house on Saturday, then a better invitation arrives. Consider a principle P1: "You may break a promise whenever a more attractive option appears." Who could reasonably reject P1? Anyone who relies on promises. Under P1, no one could ever count on another's assurance, and the ability to plan your life around others' commitments would collapse. What does the promise-breaker lose under the alternative, P2: "Keep promises unless something much more important arises, or the other person releases you"? Only the occasional better party. The objection to P1 is far stronger than the objection to P2, so P1 can be reasonably rejected, and breaking the promise is wrong. Scanlon's own analysis of promising, his **principle of fidelity**, works along these lines.

Notice what kinds of reasons count. Scanlon allows only **personal reasons**: reasons tied to the interests and standing of individuals, such as their well-being, their freedom, and their claims to fair treatment. Impersonal reasons, such as "this would produce more total happiness in the universe," are not grounds for rejecting a principle on anyone's behalf.

Scanlon also offered a striking explanation of why we care about morality at all. It is not, primarily, that wrong acts cause harm (though they often do). It is that wrong acts are ones we cannot justify to those affected, and the desire to be able to justify ourselves to others is something most people feel deeply. Wronging someone damages our relationship with them, even if they never find out.

sections.heading: Aggregation and the Transmitter Room
sections.body:
The feature that most sharply separates contractualism from utilitarianism (Day 61) is the **individualist restriction**: in judging whether a principle can be reasonably rejected, we compare the objections of *individuals*, one at a time. We do not add up small burdens on many people to outweigh a large burden on one.

Scanlon's famous illustration is the **Transmitter Room** case. Jones, a technician, has suffered an accident in the transmitter room of a television station broadcasting the World Cup final. Equipment has fallen on his arm and he is receiving extremely painful electric shocks. We can rescue him only by switching off the transmitter for fifteen minutes, which will interrupt the broadcast for millions of viewers. His injury will not get worse if we wait until the match ends an hour from now, but until then his suffering will be terrible.

A simple utilitarian adds up the disappointment of millions of fans, which could exceed Jones's suffering, and concludes we should wait. Almost everyone thinks this is the wrong answer. Contractualism explains why. Jones could reasonably reject a principle permitting us to leave him in agony for an hour; no individual viewer could reasonably reject a principle requiring the broadcast to be interrupted, because no viewer's loss is anywhere close to Jones's. The numbers of viewers do not change the size of any individual objection.

This is a powerful result. It captures the thought that each person is, as Rawls put it, separate: the suffering of one is not cancelled by the mild pleasures of many. Kant's command to treat humanity always as an end, never merely as a means, is honored.

But the restriction raises a puzzle: **do the numbers count at all?** In a classic 1977 paper, John Taurek asked whether, if you can save one person or five but not both, you are obliged to save the five. He controversially suggested you might flip a coin, since each person's loss is equally great to them. Most people think we should save the five. Scanlon offers a **tie-breaking argument**: each of the five could complain that a principle letting you save the one gives their life no weight, since the result would be the same as if they were not there. Their presence should make a difference, and it can only do so by tipping the balance. Critics question whether this argument is consistent with the individualist restriction or quietly sneaks aggregation back in.

Harder cases lie in between. Should we prevent one person's death or a million people's moderate, lasting pain? Many people's intuitions favor the million when the burdens are serious enough, which suggests that some partial aggregation is needed. Contractualists such as Alex Voorhoeve and Victor Tadros have developed theories of **partial aggregation** that count numbers when the competing burdens are of comparable seriousness, but not otherwise.

sections.heading: Objections and the Convergence Thesis
sections.body:
Contractualism faces several serious objections.

**The redundancy objection.** To decide whether a principle can be *reasonably* rejected, we need to know which objections are good ones. But surely we can know that only if we already know what is right and wrong. If so, the contract does no work; it merely restates our moral judgments in a new vocabulary. Scanlon replies that the framework is not meant to be an algorithm. It structures moral reasoning by directing attention to the burdens on individuals and to the comparative strength of their complaints, and that structure often settles questions or explains intuitions that would otherwise be puzzling, such as our verdict in the Transmitter Room.

**The scope objection.** Which beings are owed justification? Scanlon's formula concerns those who could be parties to agreement, so it seems to leave out animals and young children, the very problem that troubled contractarianism, though less severely. Scanlon proposes that we owe justification to trustees acting on behalf of beings who cannot speak for themselves, and acknowledges that some of our duties regarding animals fall outside the part of morality he calls "what we owe to each other." Critics find this a significant gap.

**Future generations.** Because the people affected by a long-term policy may not yet exist, and their very identities may depend on the policy chosen, it is hard to say what objections they could raise. This connects to the non-identity problem, which is the topic of our next lesson.

**The convergence thesis.** Derek Parfit, in *On What Matters* (2011), argued that the most defensible versions of contractualism, Kantian ethics and rule consequentialism ultimately converge on the same principles. He proposed a "Kantian contractualist" formula: everyone ought to follow the principles whose universal acceptance everyone could rationally will. Parfit then argued that these are the principles whose universal acceptance would make things go best, which is rule consequentialism. He described the three traditions as people "climbing the same mountain on different sides." Scanlon and many Kantians resisted this convergence, arguing that it erased the distinctive importance of the individual's point of view. But Parfit's project suggests that, for all the battles between moral theories you met in the 90-day course, the deep structures of moral thought may be closer than they appear.

keyQuote.text: An act is wrong if its performance under the circumstances would be disallowed by any set of principles for the general regulation of behaviour that no one could reasonably reject as a basis for informed, unforced general agreement.
keyQuote.source: T. M. Scanlon, What We Owe to Each Other (1998), chapter 4

modernConnection.title: Justifying Policies to the People Who Lose
modernConnection.body:
Public health offers a vivid test of contractualist thinking. When COVID-19 vaccines first became available in late 2020, there were far too few for everyone, and governments had to choose who would go first. A purely aggregative approach would ask which order prevents the most deaths or saves the most life-years in total. Most advisory bodies, including the United Kingdom's Joint Committee on Vaccination and Immunisation, prioritized by age and clinical risk, putting care home residents and the oldest people first because they faced by far the highest individual risk of death.

A contractualist can explain why this felt right. Ask who could reasonably reject each principle. An 85-year-old facing a high chance of death from infection has a very strong individual objection to being placed last. A healthy 25-year-old, whose personal risk was much lower, has a weaker objection to waiting. Prioritization by individual risk gives priority to those with the strongest complaints, rather than simply maximizing totals.

The same question, "Could I justify this to the person who loses out?", is increasingly asked of algorithms. When software screens job applicants or flags welfare claims as possible fraud, many people are affected by small amounts and a few by a great deal. In the Netherlands, an algorithmic system used to detect childcare benefit fraud wrongly flagged thousands of families, many with immigrant backgrounds, plunging some into severe debt; the resulting scandal led the Dutch government to resign in January 2021. Aggregate efficiency gains could not justify the devastating burden on the individuals wrongly accused. A contractualist test, centered on what each affected person could reasonably reject, makes such burdens hard to ignore.

The limits are also visible. Real policy must sometimes aggregate: cost-effectiveness analysis in health systems exists because budgets are finite, and refusing to count numbers can mean fewer lives saved. The challenge contractualism poses is not to stop counting, but to remember that every number is a person who is owed a justification.

vocabulary.definition: Scanlon's theory that an act is wrong if it is disallowed by principles that no one could reasonably reject as a basis for informed, unforced general agreement.
vocabulary.example: A contractualist asks whether the person most burdened by a rule could reasonably reject it.

vocabulary.definition: The Hobbesian view that morality consists of rules that self-interested people would agree to for mutual advantage.
vocabulary.example: Gauthier's contractarianism explains why it pays to be the kind of person who keeps agreements.

vocabulary.definition: Rejecting a principle on grounds that others, also seeking principles all can accept, would have to acknowledge as good reasons.
vocabulary.example: Someone whose life would be ruined by a rule can reasonably reject it if the alternatives burden others far less.

vocabulary.definition: Gauthier's term for a person disposed to cooperate with other cooperators even when defecting would pay in the particular case.
vocabulary.example: A constrained maximizer keeps her side of the bargain, and so is trusted with future bargains.

vocabulary.definition: The contractualist rule that principles are assessed by comparing individuals' objections one at a time, not by adding up burdens across people.
vocabulary.example: Because of the individualist restriction, millions of mildly disappointed viewers do not outweigh Jones's agony.

vocabulary.definition: Combining benefits or burdens across different people into a total, as utilitarianism does.
vocabulary.example: A policy that relieves a million headaches at the cost of one death relies on aggregation to justify itself.

vocabulary.definition: Reasons grounded in the interests, freedom or standing of particular individuals, the only reasons Scanlon allows as grounds for rejection.
vocabulary.example: 'This rule would ruin my livelihood' is a personal reason; 'this rule reduces total happiness' is not.

thinkingExercise.title: Run the Test
thinkingExercise.prompt: Apply Scanlon's reasonable rejection test to a real decision and compare it with a utilitarian approach.
steps: Choose a rule or policy that affects people unequally, at work, in your city, or online (for example, a new parking rule or a content moderation policy).
Identify the person most burdened by the rule and write down their strongest personal objection.
Write down the best alternative rule and the strongest objection someone would have to that alternative.
Compare the two objections. Which principle could be reasonably rejected? Does the answer change if you instead add up everyone's gains and losses?
Reflect: in your example, should the numbers count? If so, how would you justify that to the person who loses out?

summary: Contractarianism (Hobbes, Gauthier) grounds morality in mutual advantage among self-interested bargainers, but it struggles to give standing to those without bargaining power.
Scanlon's contractualism holds that an act is wrong if disallowed by principles no one could reasonably reject; it grounds morality in mutual justifiability rather than advantage.
The test is comparative: weigh the strongest individual objection to a principle against the strongest individual objection to the alternatives, using only personal reasons.
The individualist restriction explains the Transmitter Room verdict, but it raises the question of whether numbers count, prompting the tie-breaking argument and theories of partial aggregation.
Objections include redundancy, the scope of those owed justification, and future generations; Parfit argued that Kantian contractualism and rule consequentialism converge.

quiz.question: What is the key difference between contractarianism and contractualism?
options: Contractarianism is about the state; contractualism ignores the state
Contractarianism grounds morality in mutual advantage; contractualism in mutual justifiability
Contractarianism is Kantian; contractualism is Hobbesian
Contractualism requires an actual historical agreement
quiz.explanation: Hobbes and Gauthier ask what self-interested bargainers would agree to; Scanlon asks what principles no one could reasonably reject.

quiz.question: Which group poses the most serious problem for Gauthier-style contractarianism?
options: People with great bargaining power
Constrained maximizers
Philosophers
Beings with little bargaining power, such as infants and many animals
quiz.explanation: If morality is a deal for mutual advantage, those with nothing to offer or threaten seem to be left out.

quiz.question: On Scanlon's view, a principle is wrong to act on if anyone at all would in fact reject it.
quiz.explanation: The test is whether someone could *reasonably* reject it, not whether anyone actually would. Some people reject everything.

quiz.question: In the Transmitter Room case, why does contractualism say we should rescue Jones immediately?
options: Because rescuing him maximizes total happiness
Because Jones has a much stronger individual objection than any single viewer
Because broadcasts are not important
Because Jones agreed to a contract
quiz.explanation: Under the individualist restriction, we compare individual complaints, and no viewer's disappointment comes close to Jones's agony.

quiz.question: Which kind of reason can count as grounds for rejecting a principle, according to Scanlon?
options: Personal reasons tied to an individual's interests or standing
Impersonal reasons about total happiness in the world
Reasons of pure self-interest only
Reasons from religious authority only
quiz.explanation: Scanlon restricts the grounds of rejection to personal reasons such as well-being, freedom and fair treatment.

quiz.question: John Taurek suggested that, when choosing between saving one person and saving five, it might be acceptable to flip a coin.
quiz.explanation: In 'Should the Numbers Count?' (1977), Taurek argued that each person's loss is equally great to them, a view most people reject.

quiz.question: The 'redundancy objection' to contractualism claims that:
options: Contractualism repeats Hobbes exactly
Contractualism implies everyone has the same duties
To know what can be reasonably rejected, we must already know what is right, so the contract does no work
Contractualism has too many principles
quiz.explanation: If 'reasonable' presupposes moral knowledge, the contractualist formula may simply restate our judgments. Scanlon replies that it structures moral reasoning.

quiz.question: Derek Parfit argued that Kantian contractualism and rule consequentialism converge on the same principles.
quiz.explanation: In On What Matters, Parfit described Kantians, contractualists and consequentialists as climbing the same mountain on different sides.

quiz.question: A government gives the first scarce vaccines to the people at highest individual risk of death, rather than calculating which order maximizes total life-years. Which reasoning does this most closely follow?
options: Gauthier's constrained maximization
Taurek's coin toss
Pure aggregation
Contractualism's focus on the strongest individual objections
quiz.explanation: Prioritizing those with the strongest personal complaints, rather than maximizing totals, reflects the contractualist method.

goDeeper.body:
A lively current debate concerns **ex ante** versus **ex post** contractualism. Suppose a vaccination program will give each of a million children a tiny risk of a serious side effect, but will save many more from disease. After the fact (*ex post*), some identifiable child will have been seriously harmed, and that child seems to have a strong objection. Before the fact (*ex ante*), every child faced only a tiny risk and a large expected benefit, so no one seems to have a strong objection. Which perspective should contractualism take?

The ex ante view, defended by Sophia Reibetanz (now Moreau) and Johann Frick among others, holds that we justify principles to people as they stand when the principle is adopted, under uncertainty. This lets contractualism endorse beneficial policies that impose small risks, like vaccination programs or building roads, which seem to be clearly permissible. The ex post view, which some find in Scanlon's own writing, holds that we must take seriously the objection of the person who in fact ends up harmed. Each view handles some cases well and others badly; the ex ante view, for instance, struggles with cases in which a policy is guaranteed to harm *someone*, though no one knows who.

This debate matters well beyond philosophy. Regulators deciding on new drugs, self-driving cars or industrial safety standards must constantly impose small risks on large populations. Whether their policies are justifiable to each person depends partly on which version of the contractualist test we adopt. Scanlon's later *Being Realistic about Reasons* (2014) also connects contractualism to the metaethical questions of ethics-1, defending a modest realism about reasons that he thinks the contractualist framework requires.

readings.author: David Gauthier

readings.author: T. M. Scanlon
readings.note: The 1982 essay in Utilitarianism and Beyond (edited by Sen and Williams) that launched the theory.

questions: Can a theory based on justifying ourselves to others give adequate protection to animals and future generations?
Should the numbers count when you can save one person or five? If so, can contractualism explain why without becoming aggregative?
Is it fair to impose a tiny risk on everyone for a large shared benefit, knowing someone will be harmed?
